title: Why English says ‘father’ where Latin said ‘pater’
body: In 1786, William Jones suggested that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin sprang from a common source, now called Proto-Indo-European. Rasmus Rask and then Jacob Grimm, the elder of the fairy-tale Brothers Grimm, showed that the ancestor of the Germanic languages had shifted its consonants in regular ways. Their rule, Grimm’s law, explains why so many English words look like scrambled cousins of Latin ones.

slides.heading: p became f
slides.text: Latin pater, pes and piscis line up with English father, foot and fish. The old p sound, kept in Latin, turned into f in Germanic.

slides.heading: t became th, k became h
slides.text: Latin tres matches English three, and centum, said with a hard k, matches hundred. Latin cornu and English horn follow the same pattern.

slides.heading: d became t, g became k
slides.text: Latin decem and dens line up with ten and tooth, while genu and granum match knee and corn. The k in knee was once pronounced.

slides.heading: Why it matters
slides.text: Regular sound laws let linguists rebuild lost ancestors like Proto-Indo-European and tell true cognates from words that only look alike by chance.
